extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, judges, regulators, and legal practitioners concerned with SROs and notice-and-comment processes
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and doctrinal guidance about how courts and oversight agencies should treat self-regulatory organization (SRO) rulemaking, enforcement, and records in light of administrative law principles (notice-and-comment, deference, reviewability). Focuses on problems created by layered deference and offers doctrinal and institutional remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation limited to defined industry members
rubrics_metrics.description: Participation is open not to all “interested persons” but rather to a defined set of industry members and, perhaps, to other stakeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that consumer/public interest groups are often outnumbered or underweighted (votes diluted), producing SRO procedures that are not representative; highlights examples (NERC membership distribution, diluted consumer votes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of public-interest counterbalance in SRO structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The industry truly does develop rules to regulate itself, with little built into the SRO structure to provide a public interest counterbalance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes enforcement follows procedural due process norms but oversight agencies and outsiders criticize enforcement; absence of internal mechanisms to ensure public-interest perspectives undermines democratic legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference built into statutory and practical oversight schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Deference is built into the statutory scheme explicitly, practically, or both; oversight agencies’ authorities are frequently more limited, and even those that do have full scope rarely reject SROs’ proposed rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes how statutory design and practice create a presumption of deference to SROs, reducing agency intervention and contributing to 'double deference' when courts then defer to agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy to APA exemptions when assessing SRO procedural choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts analogize to the body of law that has developed around the APA’s similar exemptions when deciding whether an SRO has properly invoked exemption from notice-and-comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include courts treating SRO 'housekeeping' or interpretive statements similarly to agency exemptions under 5 U.S.C. §553(b)(A); courts apply standard administrative law tests to SRO procedural characterizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of rules as substantive (legislative) vs interpretive/housekeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules that go through notice-and-comment are labeled ‘substantive’ or ‘legislative’ (creating new rights or duties); policy changes, interpretive statements, or housekeeping may be exempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a purportedly exempt SRO rule effectively creates new rights/duties (e.g., FINRA's asserted authority to sue in court), courts may treat it as substantive and require full rulemaking (Fiero example).

rubrics_metrics.name: New substantive rules require full notice-and-comment
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere policy change does not necessarily require notice and comment, but when a rule creates new substantive rights or duties it should go through the full rulemaking process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fiero v. FINRA: court treated FINRA's attempt to assert court-enforcement authority as a new substantive rule that affected members' rights and thus should have undergone full notice-and-comment; courts focus on effects on rights rather than labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double deference: courts defer to agencies that defer to SROs
rubrics_metrics.description: What emerges is double deference: judicial deference to agency actions that were deferential to SROs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This layered deference often exceeds ordinary administrative-law deference because of the SROs’ expertise, and it can lead to underenforcement of administrative law norms and obscure accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts equating SROs with oversight agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: A number of courts simply equate the SRO with its oversight agency, giving no separate consideration to the relationship between the two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated in decisions that bundle the SRO and agency as one 'agency' for purposes like exhaustion and expertise; this blurring can obscure differences in roles, powers, and accountability, and invite capture concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight given to size/technicality of record over close substantive review
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may rely more on the numerous iterations of work and the size of the record than on a close look at the agency’s substantive analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes risk that agencies will amass large, technical records to obtain deference (the 'science charade'); with SROs plus agencies, records can become even more impenetrable, undermining transparency and external monitoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory design can preclude judicial review (nonreviewability)
rubrics_metrics.description: When statutes are designed to impose reviewability limitations, the impact can magnify problems; some statutory provisions preclude judicial review at particular stages (e.g., filing stage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NetCoalition II: D.C. Cir. held it lacked jurisdiction to review SEC’s refusal to suspend an SRO rule because statute provided the filing-stage action was not reviewable; nonreviewability can function as a one-way ratchet favoring industry secrecy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewability doctrines may compound SRO accountability problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewability doctrines (finality, ripeness, exhaustion, standing, zone of interests) largely do not present different barriers than in non-SRO contexts, but they may have a compounding effect in the SRO context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholder processes at SROs could create waiver or procedural obstacles; agencies (e.g., FERC) may require petitioners to explain prior presentation to SRO to avoid bypassing the process, which can impede judicial access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chenery principle: courts review only the agency’s contemporaneous rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chenery cases require that courts review an agency’s action only on the basis of the agency’s rationale at the time of its decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinguishes agency review from legislative review and promotes a structural check; courts should not supply missing reasons, and the record requirement (Overton Park) facilitates this review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include SRO record within the applicable administrative record for review
rubrics_metrics.description: In reviewing agency actions originating at the SRO level, courts should be mindful that the entire record reaches back to the SRO itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts emphasizing that the applicable standard of review includes the SRO record can enable meaningful reasoned review, promote ex ante legitimizing behavior, and encourage SROs to prepare reasoned records anticipating judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: SROs should document participatory steps and parties involved
rubrics_metrics.description: The SRO ought to document the participatory steps taken in developing the record, including whether the process was open to all interested parties and which parties participated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documentation of participation enhances transparency and allows external observers (Congress, executive, journalists, scholars) to assess procedural legitimacy; this is a quasi-procedural accountability measure rather than a waiver test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies should carefully consider significant comments raised before both the SRO and the agency
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency should carefully consider any significant comments or concerns raised before both the SRO and the agency, particularly when there has been disagreement between members, the SRO, and/or the agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requiring agencies to engage substantively with significant comments helps guard against arbitrary outcomes and strengthens accountability; particularly important where SRO and agency disagree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on imposing new procedural requirements (Vermont Yankee constraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts must be mindful of Vermont Yankee’s prohibition on imposing procedural requirements on agencies not found in the APA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although courts cannot unilaterally compel new procedures beyond the APA, lawmakers or oversight agencies might impose accountability-promoting procedures on SROs; doctrinal adjustments should account for SRO shortcomings without transgressing Vermont Yankee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political-accountability justification for deference is weaker for SROs
rubrics_metrics.description: In the ordinary administrative law context, deference is often justified by agency expertise or political accountability; for SROs, political accountability is harder to identify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oversight agencies are often independent and insulated (removal protections, multimember structures), and SROs’ internal procedures are dominated by regulated industries, so the usual political check on deference is attenuated.
